text: Cloud computing isn't one single offering — it comes in three distinct service models, and the difference between them all comes down to one simple question: how much of the technology stack does the provider manage for you, and how much is still your job? Those three models are IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, and once you can place any cloud product into one of them, the whole landscape gets a lot less confusing.

Infrastructure as a Service, like AWS EC2 or Azure Virtual Machines, hands you a virtual machine and stops there — the provider manages the physical hardware and the hypervisor underneath it, and you manage everything from the operating system up: patching, your runtime, your application, and your data. Platform as a Service, like Azure App Service or AWS Elastic Beanstalk, goes further: the provider also manages the operating system and the runtime, so you just deploy your application code and let the platform handle the server underneath it. Software as a Service, like Microsoft 365 or Salesforce, is fully managed end to end — you don't manage infrastructure, an OS, or even the application itself, just your own usage of it.

Picture the stack as six layers: datacenter hardware, virtualization, operating system, runtime, application, and data. On a plain virtual machine, you own everything from the OS upward. On a PaaS platform, the provider also owns the OS and runtime, leaving you just the application and its data. On SaaS, the provider owns everything except your data. Notice that data stays your responsibility in every single one of these models, with no exceptions — that detail is the entire subject of the next lesson.

So how do you actually choose between them? A legacy application that needs a very specific, unusual server configuration needs the full control that only IaaS gives you. A team that just wants to deploy code without running any server operations at all reaches for PaaS instead. A team that doesn't need custom software, just working email and a CRM, skips building anything and simply buys SaaS.

Next lesson: the shared responsibility model — the real framework AWS and Azure both use to spell out exactly which security tasks are always yours to handle, no matter which of these three service models you happen to be running.
